21:%%As a central idea, differential privacy requires that neighboring datasets should be almost indistinguishable.
23:%%a neighboring dataset of $\vec{x}$ is a matrix $\vec{x}'$ that differs $\vec{x}$ by one row. For example, $\vec{x}' = (x_1',\ldots, x_n)$ is a neighbor of $\vec{x}$ as %long as $x_1'\neq x_1$. What we just described is replace-one neighboring. There is also add-one/remove-one neighboring.
32:{\bf Dataset.} A dataset $S$ is a collection of $n$ records, each corresponding to an individual. Formally, we write the dataset as $S = (x_1,\ldots, x_n)$, and an individual $x_i \in X$ for some abstract space $X$. Two datasets $S' = (x'_1,\ldots, x'_n)$ and $S$ are said to be \textit{neighbors} if they differ in exactly one record, that is, there exists an index $j$ such that $x_i = x_i'$ for all $i \ne j$ and $x_j \ne x_j'$.
36:% Replace-$k$ neighboring corresponds to group privacy (see \Cref{sub:group_privacy}). In order to minimize such detail, it is helpful to make the following abstraction:
43:%%$X$ is a collection of possible instances of datasets. The neighboring relation is encoded in $\sim$. Note that a transitive $\sim$ typically does not lead to a meaningful privacy notion. \djs{More should be said on this in intro.}
52:% More precisely, when $M:X\to Y$ is fed with two neighboring datasets $x\sim x'$, the results $M(x)$ and $M(x')$ are distributions on $Y$. For example, $M:\R^{n\times d}\to\R^d$ may take the average of each column and add Gaussian noise to the average vector. $M(x)$ and $M(x')$ will be two $d$-dimensional Gaussian with different means in this case.
